finding: Round 13's repair (§6.3: "A record unit writes that file only when it is absent") contradicts unchanged §3.1.1, which states "No other kind has a file to delete. A leftover therefore either means the role is done and is not re-run, or the role is being re-run and its leftover is gone before it starts." The record kind now has a durable file whose leftover is load-bearing, and a third case exists that the dichotomy excludes: a record unit that dies after writing merged.ndjson but before the round file exists fails its §3.3 predicate, is retried, and the retry now skips the merge and re-records from a possibly partial/truncated leftover. This also breaks §10.2 invariant 17's stated retry-safety property ("a failed attempt's leftover cannot satisfy the retry's predicate") for the record kind, and reintroduces in a new place the exact harm §5 measures: a frozen, undercounted round (33 findings recorded instead of 45).
suggestion: Make the preserve rule conditional on the file being complete rather than merely present: preserve merged.ndjson only when the round was already recorded (i.e. the round file for $TP_ROUND exists) or when at least one row carries a disposition; otherwise rebuild it by merging role-*.ndjson. Update §3.1.1's "No other kind has a file to delete" sentence to name the record kind's exception, and amend invariant 17 (or add a companion invariant) so a record unit's failed attempt cannot hand a partial merge to its retry.

finding: `tp run --dry-run` and `tp run --status` have no specified exit code or side-effect contract. §3.4 pins exits only for the loop (0 on converged, 4 on every other stop_reason, 2 on a pre-loop usage error), and neither sub-mode produces a stop_reason. Tests 13 and 14 therefore cannot assert an exit code at all, and they cannot assert side effects either: it is unstated whether `--dry-run` takes the run lock at `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, creates `.tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID`, allocates a run id, or appends to `.tp/run-<base>.json`. Two engineers will write contradictory tests — one asserting `--dry-run` on an empty `next_units` exits 4 with `no-units`, another asserting it exits 0 and prints an empty list — and a spec whose premise is that the caller branches on the exit code without parsing the payload cannot leave its two read-only modes unpinned.
suggestion: State in §3.5 that `--dry-run` and `--status` exit 0 whenever they can report (including an empty unit list and an absent run state), reserve 2 for their own usage errors, and say explicitly that neither takes the run lock, allocates a run id, creates `$TP_RUN_DIR`, nor writes run state. Extend tests 13 and 14 to assert the exit code and the absence of those artifacts.

finding: §5.2 states unconditionally that a unit which wrote a valid escalation record "stops the run with `stop_reason: escalation` whatever it exited with", but §3.4's precedence list puts `converged` ahead of `escalation` and justifies it with "a cycle that became releasable is releasable whatever else the iteration also hit". When the iteration that produced an escalation record also leaves the cycle releasable, the two rules give different stop reasons, and under §3.4 the run exits 0 with a pending request for a user-only decision left unreported on disk — the opposite of §5.1's fail-closed intent, and a case §3.4's own "every non-converged stop is a report to a human" does not cover because the stop is converged.
suggestion: Pick one and state it in both places. Either place `escalation` above `converged` in §3.4's list (an outstanding user-only decision outranks a releasable cycle), or keep `converged` first and amend §5.2 to say the escalation record is reported in the run state and by `notify_cmd` even on a converged stop, so the request is never silently dropped. Add a test to §10.3 for the both-satisfied case.

finding: The new re-run rule for record units collides with test 51's failure definition and leaves `tp review/audit --record` idempotence unspecified. Test 51 makes "exit non-zero with the durable write present" a failed attempt, so a record unit that wrote `merged.ndjson`, successfully ran `--record` (round file now exists), and then had its harness exit non-zero is retried. On that retry §6.3 says the unit "re-records from" the preserved `merged.ndjson` — i.e. `--record` runs a second time for a round that is already recorded. The spec never states whether recording an already-recorded round overwrites that round entry, appends a second round, or is an error, yet convergence arithmetic (round count, clean-round streaks, `review_max_rounds`) is derived from exactly those entries. An implementer must invent the behaviour, and the wrong guess silently inflates or freezes the convergence count the driver stops on.
suggestion: State in §3.3 (or §6.3) that `tp review --record` / `tp audit --record` for a round number that already has a round file is idempotent — it replaces that round's entry rather than appending a new one — and add a test under 10.2 asserting that a retried record unit leaves the recorded round count unchanged.

finding: Test 5 asserts concurrency "from the seam's recorded spawn and exit timestamps", which is not a deterministic test. Nothing in §3.2.1's `TP_RUNNER_SEAM` contract makes a fake unit hold its process open, so a sequential implementation can produce spawn/exit timestamps that overlap within clock resolution, and a genuinely parallel run on a loaded machine can produce disjoint ones. The test as specified therefore both false-passes and false-fails, and the negative half ("every other kind does not overlap them") is worse: proving non-overlap from timestamps requires the serial units to take measurable time, which the seam is designed not to do.
suggestion: Give the seam a blocking primitive — e.g. the fake runner waits on a file or a barrier until released — and restate test 5 as an assertion on observed simultaneity (two role units alive at once, proved by the barrier) and on strict ordering for serial kinds (the second kind's spawn is never recorded before the first's exit), rather than on timestamp comparison.

finding: Test 24 is not a deterministic pass/fail test on two counts. It requires the plugin to validate with `claude plugin validate`, which makes the outcome depend on an external CLI being installed on the machine, on its version, and on validation rules tp does not control — a test that fails when the tool is missing and silently passes (or is skipped) when it is, with no stated behaviour for either case. And "its hook payloads are asserted against fixtures" names neither which payloads nor what the fixtures contain; the only payload the spec pins anywhere is the `SessionStart` hook's ("`tp resume --compact` and nothing else", §6.2), while the `PreToolUse` deny decision and the `Stop` block reason have no documented payload shape to assert against.
suggestion: Split test 24: make the `claude plugin validate` run an explicitly optional, skipped-when-absent check (or replace it with a schema assertion tp owns over `plugin.json` and `hooks/`), and enumerate the hook payloads under test — SessionStart additional-context, PreToolUse deny decision, Stop block reason — pinning the required fields of each in §6.2.

finding: Test 34 — "Two simultaneously satisfied stop conditions record the higher-precedence reason" — names no pair, while §3.4 defines a total order over eight reasons (28 pairs). Two engineers will implement entirely different tests, and the pairs whose ordering is least obvious and most consequential can go untested by both: `escalation` before `unit-failure` (a unit that escalated and also failed its predicate), `cap-budget` before `cap-wall-clock` (both tripped in the same checkpoint), and `no-units` last (an empty `next_units` on the same iteration a cap trips). The one pair the prose does argue for, `converged` first, is also the one an implementation gets right for free because §3.1 checks releasability first.
suggestion: Enumerate in test 34 the specific pairs that must be asserted — at minimum converged/cap-units, escalation/unit-failure, cap-budget/cap-wall-clock, and no-units against any cap — so the test pins the order rather than a single arbitrary instance of it.

finding: `TP_UNIT_SEQ` composes two literal filenames — the log path `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` (§3.5) and the escalation record `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` (§5.2) — yet its form is never pinned: whether it starts at 0 or 1, and whether it is zero-padded. §3.5's example row shows `"seq": 0` alongside `"attempt": 1`, which reads as two different origins for two adjacent counters and invites the opposite guess. Test 37 enumerates the forms of `TP_RUN_ID`, `TP_RUN_DIR`, `TP_ROUND_DIR` and `TP_FILE` but omits `TP_UNIT_SEQ`, `TP_UNIT_ID` and `TP_UNIT_KIND` entirely, so any test asserting a first-unit log path (`0-implement-x.jsonl` vs `1-implement-x.jsonl`) is a coin flip.
suggestion: State in §3.1.1 that `seq` is a decimal integer starting at 1 (or 0), unpadded, and that `attempt` starts at 1, then extend test 37 to cover `TP_UNIT_SEQ`, `TP_UNIT_ID` and `TP_UNIT_KIND` and assert the literal log and escalation filenames of the first unit.

finding: §3.1.1 introduces a new runtime artifact, `.tp/locks/run-<base>.lock`, held for the whole run. §10.2 test 15 enumerates the git-ignored set as `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, and §10.7 states the `.tp/.gitignore` fixture "gains four entries" — `.tp/locks/` is in neither. Since `.tp/` is otherwise a committed directory (`config.json`, `reviewers/`, `auditors/`), an unattended run leaves the lock file as untracked noise in every working tree it touches.
suggestion: Either add `.tp/locks/` to the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` (making it five entries in §10.7 and in test 15), or state that `.tp/locks/` is already covered by an existing ignore rule and cite it.

finding: §3.2.2 requires two run-start reports — that `run_max_budget_usd` is inert for a runner declaring no `spend_key` is "reported once at run start, not silently", and that under a per-kind map "the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered" — but neither has a pinned surface (stdout, stderr, or a field of `.tp/run-<base>.json` / `--status`) or a pinned shape, and no test in §10 asserts either. Test 11 asserts only that `spend` is null and `cap-budget` inert, which an implementation that reports nothing at run start passes. A requirement whose whole point is that a partial total is never mistaken for a complete one cannot be verified without naming where the operator sees it.
suggestion: Name the stream and the shape of the run-start report in §3.2.2 (e.g. one stderr line plus an `unmetered_kinds[]` field carried by `tp run --status`), and extend test 11 to assert it for both the no-`spend_key` case and the per-kind map with a mix of metered and unmetered kinds.

finding: The `decompose` kind's durable write is "The task file holds at least one task", and §3.3 requires every predicate to be a state with no baseline. For this kind the two combine into a predicate no test can falsify in the case that matters: a first attempt that imports tasks and then exits non-zero is a failed attempt, and the retry that follows satisfies the predicate whether or not it does anything at all, because the earlier attempt's tasks are still there. The same holds for any re-run of `tp run` after a partially completed decompose. Test 18 asserts only the general property ("decidable from one file with no baseline") and its `audit-fix` instance, so nothing in §10 exercises the decompose retry path, and no test can distinguish a no-op decompose unit from a working one.
suggestion: Either strengthen the decompose predicate to something a retry can fail (e.g. the task file holds at least one task **and** the oracle's phase has advanced past decompose), or state explicitly in §3.3 that a decompose retry on a non-empty task file is treated as already satisfied and skipped rather than re-attempted — then add the retry case to test 18.

finding: §4.1 defines `round` only as "the phase's current round number", which reads equally as the last *recorded* round and as the in-flight, not-yet-recorded one. The two readings differ by one and both are load-bearing: §3.1.1 derives `TP_ROUND_DIR` = `<phase>-r$TP_ROUND` (the directory collecting the in-flight round's role files), while §3.3 makes the record unit's predicate "a review round file for `$TP_ROUND` exist". Under the last-recorded reading the record predicate is satisfied before the unit runs and the role files land in the previous round's directory; under the in-flight reading both are correct. Nothing in §4.1, §3.1.1 or §3.3 disambiguates, and a one-off here makes the record unit either a no-op or permanently failing.
suggestion: Define `round` in §4.1 as the round being worked — last recorded round + 1 in a round-based phase — and state that `tp review --record`/`tp audit --record` write exactly that number, so the driver's `TP_ROUND` and the predicate agree by construction. Add an assertion to test 38 or 36 pinning the relationship.

finding: Two normative clauses of §5.1 have no test in §10.3. (a) The activation predicate — the mode is active when `TP_UNATTENDED` is "present, non-empty and not `0`" — is a three-part rule, but test 19 exercises only `=1` and the variable absent; the discriminating cases (`TP_UNATTENDED=`, `TP_UNATTENDED=0`, `TP_UNATTENDED=false`) are untested, and an implementation that treats any presence as active passes every test as written. (b) The accepted-0 direction — "setting 0 where 0 already resolves changes nothing and is accepted" — is untested; test 19 covers only the refused direction (0 while a non-zero value resolves exits 2) and the accepted direction only for "an equal or lower non-zero value", which excludes 0 by its own wording.
suggestion: Extend test 19 to enumerate the activation predicate (`1`, `true`, empty, `0`, unset) with the expected active/inactive outcome for each, and to assert that setting a budget field to 0 while 0 already resolves exits 0.

finding: §5.1 fences `notify_cmd` "at any layer" under `TP_UNATTENDED`, and the four fenced rows in its table are all `tp set --workflow` / `tp done` / `tp import` operations. But §7 says `notify_cmd` is per-operator and "read from `.tp/local.json` only" — the layer `tp set --workflow` does not write. The fence therefore refuses an operation that could not have taken effect anyway, while the one layer the driver actually reads has no named command and no stated refusal. Test 40 ("`runner` and `notify_cmd` cannot be set at any layer") has no write path to exercise for the layer that matters.
suggestion: Name the command that writes `.tp/local.json` defaults, state that it refuses `notify_cmd` (and `runner`) under `TP_UNATTENDED` with the same exit 2 and hint shape, and point test 40 at that command rather than at `tp set --workflow`.

finding: "When an iteration produces several [escalation records], the driver reports the lowest `seq` and preserves them all" names no surface on which that report appears. §3.5's run-state schema has no escalation field, `--status`'s enumerated contents do not include an escalation path, and only `notify_cmd` is documented to receive `TP_ESCALATION_PATH`. Test 22 asserts only that two concurrent siblings each write their own record. So the selection rule — lowest `seq` — is unobservable in every documented output, and no test can distinguish an implementation that picks the lowest from one that picks the first or the highest, except indirectly through `notify_cmd`, which test 42 does not tie to the multi-record case.
suggestion: State that `TP_ESCALATION_PATH` and `tp run --status` both carry the lowest-`seq` record's path, and extend test 22 (or 42) to produce two concurrent escalation records and assert that the reported path is the lower `seq` while both files remain on disk.

finding: "A record unit writes that file only when it is absent" has no owner. `--merge` prints to stdout, so `merged.ndjson` is produced by the unit's own redirection; if the presence check lives only in the brief prose, nothing enforces it — and §3.1/Non-Goal 6 make prose the one thing the driver will not rely on, so a retry that clobbers `merged.ndjson` destroys the dispositions test 57 requires preserved with no observable failure. Nor is the write required to be atomic, unlike the run-state writes §3.5 explicitly makes temp+rename, so a unit killed mid-redirect leaves a truncated `merged.ndjson` that the retry then preserves as authoritative.
suggestion: Give the invariant a tp-side owner: have `tp review --merge` / `tp audit --merge` accept an output path that refuses to overwrite an existing file (or is a no-op when it exists) and writes it atomically (temp + rename), and state that the record unit uses that flag rather than shell redirection. Extend test 57 to cover a truncated pre-existing `merged.ndjson`.

finding: The repair makes a re-run record unit "re-record from" a merged.ndjson that by then accumulates dispositions from review-resolve and audit-fix, but no section says how a disposed row counts at --record time. §3.3 notes --record counts non-PASS rows for convergence and §5 treats the recorded count as frozen evidence; if disposed rows are excluded (or counted) differently than on the first pass, a re-run silently rewrites an already-frozen round's count in the direction that flatters convergence — the same class of inflated convergence count §8a already routes to this spec.
suggestion: State explicitly in §6.3 (and mirror as an invariant beside 57) that re-recording a round is idempotent with respect to its recorded finding count: dispositions on rows do not change what --record counts, and re-recording an already-recorded round leaves the frozen count unchanged.

finding: §6.3 makes `merged.ndjson` write-once — "A record unit writes that file only when it is absent" — and §3.3 makes its mere existence the record unit's durable-write predicate, while §3.3 (`review-resolve`, `audit-fix`) and §6.3 make it the accumulating home of dispositions. No section requires that write to be atomic. A record unit killed mid-write (driver death, wall-clock overshoot, SIGTERM per §3.4) leaves a truncated file that satisfies the existence predicate and that the retry is forbidden to overwrite, so the round is recorded from a partial merge. §3.5 mandates temp + rename for the run-state file it explicitly calls "observability, not truth"; the file that is truth gets no such rule.
suggestion: Require `merged.ndjson` to be written temp + rename, so it is either absent or complete, and say so in §6.3 next to the write-once rule. Add an invariant to §10.6 asserting a truncated merge cannot satisfy the record unit's predicate.

finding: §6.3 puts "the escalation record `tp escalate` writes on their behalf" inside the reviewer/auditor write allowlist, and test 55 asserts the definitions "permit writing only the role's own findings file and its escalation record, and deny every other path". A Claude Code agent's tool restrictions govern the file-writing tools; the escalation record is written by a `tp` subprocess, not by `Write`/`Edit`. It therefore neither needs nor can receive an allowlist entry — and since a role unit must run its `brief_command` and `tp escalate` through a shell tool, every path restriction in the definition is already bypassable by the same route §6.2 deliberately leaves outside its matcher. As written, test 55 asserts a property the mechanism cannot have.
suggestion: Split the two channels explicitly, as §6.2 already does for the deny hook: the tool allowlist covers file-writing tools and names only `$TP_ROUND_DIR/role-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`; the escalation record is written by tp through the shell and is out of the allowlist's scope. Restate test 55 over the file-writing tools only.

finding: §6.3 requires the `tp-reviewer`/`tp-auditor` definitions to "permit writing only the role's own findings file and its escalation record" and test 55 pins it, but the spec never names the mechanism, and the two named paths are not expressible the same way. Agent definitions scope *tools*, not paths; path-scoped denial elsewhere in this spec is done by a `PreToolUse` hook (§6.2). Worse, the escalation record is written by `tp escalate` — a Bash-invoked subprocess — so no Write/Edit allowlist entry can cover it, and §6.2 itself concedes shell tools are outside the matcher. The findings path also contains `$TP_ROUND_DIR`/`$TP_UNIT_ID`, which are per-unit environment values rather than static globs. As written, the implementer cannot tell what artifact to author or what test 55 asserts against.
suggestion: Name the concrete construct in §6.3 (e.g. permission rules with `Write(...)`/`Edit(...)` specifiers in the agent definition, using a static glob such as `.tp/rounds/**/role-*.ndjson`), and state explicitly that writes performed by tp itself through Bash — including `tp escalate`'s record — are outside the tool allowlist and are governed by `tp escalate`'s own path derivation. Restate test 55 against whatever that construct is.

finding: Test 16 requires each §7 field to "accept both range endpoints, and reject one step outside each", but for the three decimal-dollar fields "one step" is undefined: §7 says only "Budget fields are decimal dollars" and pins no precision or rounding. For `run_max_budget_usd` (0-10000) the rejected value below the floor is -1, -0.01, or -0.001 depending on the engineer, and above the ceiling 10001 or 10000.01; whether 10000.004 is accepted-and-rounded or rejected is likewise unstated. The same test also cannot be written for `runner` ("Built-in name or object") and `notify_cmd` ("Any command string"), which have no endpoints at all, yet test 16 says "each §7 field".
suggestion: Pin the decimal precision of the budget fields (e.g. two decimal places, values outside the range rejected on the exact-cent boundary) and state the rejection values the test must use; and exempt `runner` and `notify_cmd` from the endpoint clause of test 16, naming instead what an invalid value is for each.

finding: The `location_clusters` entry `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` is not pinned well enough for a deterministic assertion. Three things are open: whether `roles[]` and `severities[]` are deduplicated or carry one element per contributing finding; their ordering (input order, sorted, or role-corpus order); and what `count` counts — findings at that location or roles at it. The inclusion rule is also ambiguous against `count`: the entry exists "per `location` carrying findings from more than one role", so a location with three findings from a single role must be excluded, but nothing says so where a reader looking at `count` would see it. Test 28 asserts only that a location reported by two roles under different classes is grouped, so every one of these choices goes unverified and two engineers write contradictory assertions.
suggestion: Give §8a.1 an example entry with literal values, state that `roles[]` and `severities[]` are deduplicated and sorted (naming the order), define `count` as the number of findings at the location, and state explicitly that a location whose findings all come from one role produces no entry. Add that exclusion case to test 28.

finding: Test 30 asserts a truncated set reports `truncated` true and `total_changed` above `total_files`, but never tests the cap boundary itself. The cap is 50, so the discriminating cases are exactly 50 changed files (`truncated` false, `total_changed == total_files == 50`) and 51 (`truncated` true, `total_files` 50). As written the test passes against an implementation whose comparison is `>= 50` and against one whose comparison is `> 50`, which is the off-by-one this project's own mutation-testing lesson names — a rule verified with a value far outside the boundary is verified whether the bound is inclusive or exclusive.
suggestion: Split test 30 into the 50-file case (truncated false, both counts 50, no notice) and the 51-file case (truncated true, total_files 50, total_changed 51, notice naming both numbers), asserting the payload under `--quiet` in both.

finding: Two coverage gaps in the phase and kind enumerations. Test 2 asserts the loop "advances through implement, review and audit phases", omitting `decompose`, which §3.3 lists as a kind and §4.1 implies as a phase between review and implement — so the phase transition most likely to be mis-ordered is outside the end-to-end test. And of §3.3's eight kinds, `review-resolve` is the only one whose durable-write predicate ("Every finding in `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson` carries a disposition") is named by no test in §10; test 57 covers the record unit's preservation of those dispositions but not the resolve unit's own success condition, including the case where a finding carries a disposition already written by an earlier attempt.
suggestion: Extend test 2 to walk the full phase sequence including decompose, and add a test asserting the `review-resolve` predicate directly: a merged file with one undisposed finding fails the unit, and a file where every finding carries a disposition passes, whichever attempt wrote them.

finding: Test 15 and §10.7 require the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` to gain four entries, given as `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`, but a gitignore fixture assertion needs literal strings and these are neither literal nor in the file's own form: the existing file holds entries relative to `.tp/` (`local.json`, `locks/`), and two of the four are parameterised by `<base>`, so they must ship as globs whose exact spelling (`run-*.json` vs `/run-*.json` vs `run-*.tasks.json`) the spec never states. An engineer writing the fixture has to invent the strings the test then asserts.
suggestion: Quote the four literal lines as they will appear in `.tp/.gitignore` (relative form, glob spelling included) in §10.7, so the fixture assertion has a single correct answer.
